name: There were no burgers of the day in this episode but in the Hugo's Hot Dogs segment a Hot Dog of the Day appeared which was the "View to a Kielbasa Dog" which is a reference to the 1985 James Bond movie "A View to a Kill."

recipe.history:
Kielbasa — from the Polish word for sausage, itself descending from the Turkish word for roasted meat — is one of the great sausage traditions of Eastern Europe, with roots stretching back to medieval Poland where guilds of butchers prepared pork and beef forcemeat seasoned with garlic, marjoram, and smoke in quantities sufficient to last through the brutal winters of the Vistula plain. The most iconic form, kielbasa wędzona, is a smoked pork sausage with a firm, snappy casing and a deep mahogany exterior, its flavor shaped by the wood smoke of oak or alder that has been curing it for hours or days. Polish culinary tradition treats kielbasa not as a secondary player but as a centerpiece — served with rye bread, mustard, and pickled cucumber, or simmered in bigos, the hunter's stew of sauerkraut, mushrooms, and braised meats that is arguably Poland's national dish. Every Polish region has its own variation: the thin, garlic-heavy biała kielbasa of Kraków, the coarse-ground kabanosy of eastern Poland, the horseshoe-shaped kiełbasa śląska of Silesia. It is a tradition of specificity, of terroir expressed through casing and smoke.

Kielbasa arrived in American kitchens in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries alongside the massive waves of Polish, Czech, Slovak, and Ukrainian immigrants who settled in the industrial cities of the Midwest and Northeast — Chicago, Cleveland, Detroit, Pittsburgh, and Milwaukee. These communities brought their sausage-making traditions intact, establishing butcher shops and smokehouse operations that became neighborhood institutions. The kielbasa cookout — a sausage grilled outdoors, sliced into coins, and served with mustard and beer — became a fixture of Midwestern backyard culture regardless of ancestry. By the latter half of the twentieth century, kielbasa had transcended its ethnic origins and entered the mainstream American pantry. Innovative cooks and restaurateurs, seeing kielbasa's potential for deep, smoky flavor, began incorporating it into burgers either as a secondary protein layer, crumbled into the patty mix, or as a grilled slice alongside the beef — a nod to its hot dog cousin without abandoning the burger format that Bob's kitchen demands.

The first time I cooked kielbasa properly — not just sliced and microwaved from a package, which is frankly a crime — was at a block party in Hamtramck, Michigan, the old Polish enclave within Detroit that still smells like garlic and smoke if you walk through it on a summer evening. A neighbor named Mr. Kowalczyk grilled rings of kielbasa over charcoal and then let them rest on a cutting board, sliced them thick on the diagonal, and handed me a piece with a smear of stone-ground mustard. The casing snapped. The smoke hit the back of my throat before the meat did. The garlic and marjoram were not subtle — they announced themselves and then settled into the fat. I went back to that cutting board four more times that afternoon, and I have never forgotten what properly smoked kielbasa tastes like when it's been treated with the respect it deserves.

The philosophy of medium rare extends beyond pure beef, and in this kielbasa-inspired burger it informs how we treat every component. The beef patty, cooked to an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — remains juicy, pink, and rich, its fat still molten and carrying flavor. The kielbasa, already fully cooked and smoked by its preparation, is seared until its casing crackles and its exterior chars slightly, adding a layer of textural and flavor complexity that medium-rare beef alone cannot provide. The result is a burger that honors both traditions: the Polish sausage-maker's commitment to smoke, spice, and preservation, and the American burger cook's insistence that a patty cooked past medium rare is a patty that has given up. We do not give up here.
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680g) 80/20 ground chuck, freshly ground if possible
8 oz (225g) smoked kielbasa sausage, sliced into 1/4-inch coins
1 cup sauerkraut, drained and lightly squeezed
1 small yellow onion, halved and thinly sliced
Dill pickles, sliced lengthwise, for serving
instructions: 1. Make the mustard-horseradish sauce: in a small bowl, whisk together the stone-ground mustard, mayonnaise, prepared horseradish, apple cider vinegar, and brown sugar until smooth. Taste and adjust seasoning. Cover and refrigerate.

2. Cook the caraway onions: melt the butter in a skillet over medium heat. Add the sliced yellow onion, caraway seeds, and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 20 to 25 minutes until the onions are deep golden brown and very soft. Add a splash of water if the pan looks dry. Set aside.

3. Warm the sauerkraut: add the drained sauerkraut to the skillet after removing the onions, over medium-low heat. Toss with a pinch of caraway and a small amount of the onion fond left in the pan. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until heated through and slightly dried out. Set aside.

4. Sear the kielbasa: heat 1 tablespoon of oil in a cast iron skillet over medium-high heat. Add the kielbasa coins in a single layer. Sear without moving for 2 to 3 minutes per side until deeply browned and slightly charred at the edges. Transfer to a plate. Do not discard the rendered fat in the pan.

5. Form the patties: combine the ground chuck with garlic powder, marjoram, smoked paprika, crushed caraway, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, and 1/2 teaspoon black pepper. Mix gently until just combined. Divide into 4 portions and form into patties approximately 3/4 inch thick with a dimple pressed into the center of each.

6. Cook the patties: heat the remaining 1 tablespoon of oil in the same cast iron skillet over high heat, keeping any rendered kielbasa fat in the pan for added flavor. Cook the patties without moving for 3 to 4 minutes until a firm, dark crust develops on the underside.

7. Flip each patty once. Immediately lay a slice of Swiss or Gruyère cheese on each. Cook for 2 to 3 more minutes, checking with an instant-read thermometer. Remove patties when the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). This is medium rare — the exact temperature window for maximum juiciness and flavor. Do not cook further.
8. Transfer patties to a wire rack and rest for 3 to 5 minutes.
9. Toast the pretzel buns: split and toast in a dry skillet or under a broiler until warm and slightly crisped on the cut face.

10. Assemble: spread the mustard-horseradish sauce on both bun halves. On the bottom bun, place a layer of warm sauerkraut, then the rested patty with melted cheese, then a generous spoonful of caraway onions, and finally 3 to 4 seared kielbasa coins arranged across the top. Add dill pickle slices on the side or directly on the burger. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
